new_statements.quote: 2.—In words where no syllabic accent is used the stress of the voice always rests on the first syllable of a word; e.g., "Faidang" = "fai'dang"; "Faidangman" = "fai'dangman," &c. This rule holds good even in words where the second (or later) syllable of a word contains a long vowel whilst the first syllable has only a short one, accent being to some extent independent of the quantity of vowel sounds; e.g., "Mosa" (tiger) = "mo'sa," &c. Exception.—In adjectives beginning with "ga" the second syllable is almost always the accented one; e.g., "Gaza" (red) = "gaza'." 3.—In words of more than two syllables the accent, as a general rule, rests on the last syllable but one (penultimate).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, PDF pp. 49-50 = printed pp. 7-8, rendered at 100 dpi and read from the page images (also djvu text lines 3555-3610). Rules 2-5 under "General Rules relating to Accent, &c." are there as quoted; the only differences are diacritics the reader's transcription dropped: the scan prints "Gă", "Găzá'" (red), "Mosá" (tiger) = "mo'sá", "Mosá'ni". The secondary-accent passage (Thang'-ni-au''-nu, main accent third syllable, secondary first, final -nu "a kind of enclitic") is on printed p. 6 (PDF p. 48) as reported. new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables are stressed on the first syllable and longer words on the penultimate, which together amount to penultimate stress; the examples given for suffixed nouns (Mo'sa ~ Mosa'ni 'of a tiger'), polysyllabic verb roots (ga-glai'-nu 'to fall', ge-le'-nu 'to play') and enclitic-final forms (accent on the syllable before the enclitic) all fall on the penult. Adjectives with the prefix ga- are stressed on the second (final) syllable instead.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Endle p. 6: in long words two accented syllables are marked, a main (double mark) and a secondary (single mark); e.g. Thang'-ni-au''-nu 'even while going' has the main accent on the third syllable and the secondary on the first (the final -nu being 'a kind of enclitic').
new_statements.exceptions: ga- adjectives accent the second syllable (gaza' 'red'); a noun accented on its first syllable may shift the accent to its second when case endings are appended (Mo'sa > Mosa'ni); verbs mostly keep the root accent (first syllable) through conjugation, but in compound verbs the second member takes the accent (khat'-bai vs khat-hing'-bai); verbal roots of more than one syllable accent the second syllable; the enclitics nu and sui put the accent on the syllable immediately preceding them; adjectives in ga- have an ultra-short first vowel (gza, gfut).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement on citation forms and inflected words of Darrang Kachari in 1884, written before tone was recognised in the language; Endle's 'accent' may partly reflect tone. Later phonological work is tonal: Burton-Page 1955 (Gauhati speaker) posits three tones and states that 'intonation and stress are more conveniently considered as abstractions from units longer than the syllable, and are thus excluded in principle from this paper' (p. 341), while noting unstressed, voiceless-vowel initial syllables in words like pi'sa 'son', si'kla 'young girl', ku'ga 'bird's beak' (pp. 336-337); Joseph & Burling 2006 find two tones on monosyllables and could not analyse polysyllables (pp. 17-19); Samy 2011 gives two tones and nothing on stress (p. 521); Das 2017 (abstract) describes Boro as a two-tone language whose lexical tones align to the right edge of a minimal disyllabic prosodic word.
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit stress-placement statement found is Endle 1884, which describes the Kachari (Bara = Bodo) of District Darrang, Assam, as spoken in the 1880s (Burton-Page 1955 fn. 1 notes that the Darrang dialect 'differs from that recorded here [Gauhati] in several particulars'). Glottolog 5.1 lists only Mech [mech1238] and Chote [chot1240] as dialects of bodo1269; Darrang Kachari has no separate glottocode. Modern standard Bodo is the western (Kokrajhar) variety. All later descriptions (Burton-Page 1955, Joseph & Burling 2006, Samy 2011, Das 2017) treat Boro as a tone language (2-3 tones) and none states a word-stress rule; Burton-Page explicitly excludes stress from his analysis.

sources.citation: Joseph, U. V. & Robbins Burling. 2006. The comparative phonology of the Boro-Garo languages. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. (archive.org dli.language.0865)
sources.note: 'Boro Tones' pp. 17-19: two-way tone contrast (high, short, glottal-stopped vs low, longer) on monosyllables; the authors could not extend the analysis to polysyllables; rejects Burton-Page's three and Bhattacharya's four tones. The only 'stress' remarks in the book concern Tiwa and Garo; nothing on Boro word stress.
